power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

Language Background was not significant (B = 0.03, SE = 0.17, z = 0.17, p = .87), meaning that multilingual speakers neither benefited nor suffered detectably overall from their more diverse language experiences.

Additionally, none of the 11 interaction terms involving Language Background were significant, including Language Background x Accent (B = 0.20, SE = 0.30, z = 0.69, p = .49), suggesting that being multilingual did not confer selective advantages for accented speech.

table.formatted: One interaction was marginal, Context x Sentence Type x Language Background (B = 1.42, SE = 0.73, z = 1.93, p = .053), suggesting that the relative sensicalsentence context benefit was slightly milder for multilingual listeners (see Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure">S6</ref>).
table.expanded: One interaction was marginal, Context x Sentence Type x Language Background (B = 1.42, SE = 0.73, z = 1.93, p = .053), suggesting that the relative sensicalsentence context benefit was slightly milder for multilingual listeners (see Supplementary Figure S6).

Sensicality interacted (B = -0.30, SE = 0.14, z = -2.13, p = .03), not observed in human transcribers, such that words from sensical sentences were more accurate overall but the benefit was larger for Spanish accents than US English accents.

This was qualified by a 3-way interaction of Accent, Sentence Sensicality, and Context (B = -1.04, SE = 0.28, z = -3.72, p = .0002), also absent in human data, such that the sentence-context boost for sensical over nonsensical/nonword sentences was relatively greater for Spanish accents.

This three-way interaction was further qualified by a four-way interaction with Whisper Size (B = -0.46, SE = 0.19, z = -2.43, p = .02), such that the greater sentence benefit for sensical sentences did not change in magnitude for US accents as model size increased (B = -0.22, SE = 0.20, z = -1.12, p = .26), but increased in magnitude for Spanish accents as model size increased (B = 0.25, SE = 0.07, z = 3.57, p = .0004). in sentences (solid) and in isolation) dotted.

A three-way interaction seen in the Whisper size results was also evident here: Accent x high Sentence Sensicality x Context (B = -0.99, SE = 0.45, z = -2.22, p = .03).
The Transcriber main effect was significant (B = 0.27, SE = 0.13, z = 2.08, p = .04), suggesting a mild advantage for Whisper-large overall.

Transcriber and the low Sentence Sensicality contrast interacted (B = -0.53, SE = 0.22, z = -2.42, p = .02), such that human transcribers did worse in nonword-containing sentences than nonsensical ones, while the model did not.
Transcriber also interacted with Context (B = 1.05, SE = 0.43, z = 2.47, p = .01), with a larger sentence-context benefit for models than humans.
Further, there was a four-way Transcriber x Context x high Sentence Sensicality x Accent interaction (B = -1.98, SE = 0.89, z = -2.23, p = .03).

However, for the nonsensical/nonword sentences, humans and model differed, with a Transcriber x Context interaction (B = 1.39, SE = 0.51, z = 2.69, p = .007) and a Transcriber x Context x Accent interaction (B = 0.92, SE = 0.41, z = 2.22, p =.03).

However, for the nonsensical/nonword sentences, humans and model differed, with a Transcriber x Context interaction (B = 1.39, SE = 0.51, z = 2.69, p = .007) and a Transcriber x Context x Accent interaction (B = 0.92, SE = 0.41, z = 2.22, p =.03).

Humans showed no sentence context boost for nonsensical/nonword sentences (B = 0.12, SE = 0.16, z = 0.73, p = .47) and the lack of context boost did not differ by accent (B = -0.09, SE = 0.25, z = -0.38, p = .71).

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 169 columns across 13 data files.
#### Issues Identified

23 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 13 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("Final WER analysis and figs OSF.R", 
"Sentence stem autoscore analysis and figs OSF.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—"), Basis = c("none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `transcriberinfo.txt` to `transcriberInfo.txt` (in Final WER analysis and figs OSF.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.

**1 file name in the code is not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Final WER analysis and figs OSF.R", "Name in the code" = "transcriberinfo.txt", 
    "Name in the deposit" = "transcriberInfo.txt"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Final WER analysis and figs OSF.R", 
"Sentence stem autoscore analysis and figs OSF.R"), Outcome = c("timed_out", 
"ran_ok"), Detail = c("timeout", ""), "Time (s)" = c(300.4, 106.5
)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```

2 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. text.text: Despite advancements in speech recognition technology, questions remain about model generalizability and how much models mirror human recognition.
These questions are addressed by comparing OpenAI's Whisper model and 75 human transcribers on 300 English sentences (20 speakers, half F, half M, half US-accented, half Spanish-accented).

Sentences ended in 100 target words, each occurring in one sensical sentence (The monkey ate the banana), one nonsensical (The monkey ate the shark), and one nonsensical+nonword (The runkey ate the shark).
Target word transcription accuracy was examined both in sentences and in isolation (recordings excised from same sentences).
Human transcriptions replicated existing work.
There were two major findings.
First, the model transcribed Spanish-accented speech less well, and it benefited from sensical contexts, particularly for Spanish-accented speech.

Second, sentence context affected models differently than humans: humans benefited only from sensical sentences (final words insentence more accurate than in isolation), while Whisper benefited from any sentence context.

Humans and Whisper showed similar patterns of talker difficulty, but different error patterns on isolated words, possibly due to Whisper's word-prediction model being overly restrictive in short utterances.
Suggestions for ASR development, and the possible practical and scientific contributions of ASR to understanding human accent processing is discussed.
How well do automatic speech recognition (ASR) models generalize outside their training data?

A few recent studies suggest that at least one model, OpenAI's Whisper (Radford et al., 2023) performs comparably to human transcribers (Radford et al., 2023) on second-language English speech (Mandarin accents: Kim et al., 2024; Japanese accents: McGuire & Larson-Hall, 2025;  though see Graham and Roll, 2024).
text.formatted: A few recent studies suggest that at least one model, OpenAI's Whisper <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref> performs comparably to human transcribers <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref> on second-language English speech (Mandarin accents: <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kim et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Japanese accents: McGuire & Larson-Hall, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Graham and Roll, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It is not clear what factors contribute to ASR model success, or whether the accented speech outcomes for some accents generalize to additional less-trained accents or speech varieties.
Here we assess the performance of one ASR system, Whisper, on yet another accent of English, Spanish-accented English.

We assess the extent to which the ASR system benefits from sentence context by comparing transcription accuracy of sentence-final words when presented with vs. without preceding sentence context, where sentences are either sensical or anomalous.
We use human transcribers and US-accented English as baselines.

Underlying the question of model performance is the extent to which ASR systems are good analogs to human speech processing, so we also compare transcription performance directly between the largest Whisper model and humans.
Every speaker has an accent.
Accents are relative differences in segmental and suprasegmental sound patterns in a language which can result from differences in region of origin (e.g.
Scottishaccented English vs.
US-accented English, or Southern US-accented English vs.
Northeastern US-accented English), first language (e.g.
US-accented English vs.
Spanish-accented English or Mandarin-accented English), or social group variation (white Southern-accented English varieties vs.
African-American English varieties).
If a listener does not use or at least regularly hear the accent, they have increased difficulty recognizing what was said (see, e.g., Bradlow & Bent 2008; Cristià et al., 2012).
text.formatted: If a listener does not use or at least regularly hear the accent, they have increased difficulty recognizing what was said (see, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bradlow & Bent 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cristià et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Stronger accents, that is, those more distant from the listener's own accent, are relatively more difficult (e.g. Bradlow & Bent, 2008; Kim et al., 2024; Sidaras et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Stronger accents, that is, those more distant from the listener's own accent, are relatively more difficult (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bradlow & Bent, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kim et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sidaras et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: While many sound features vary between accents, phonetic Levenshtein distance or edit distance-the proportion of speech sounds in an utterance that differ from those in the speaker's accent-has been shown to predict both word recognition (Bent et al., 2021) and accentedness rankings (Henry et al., 2024) in children and adults.
text.formatted: While many sound features vary between accents, phonetic Levenshtein distance or edit distance-the proportion of speech sounds in an utterance that differ from those in the speaker's accent-has been shown to predict both word recognition <ref type="bibr">(Bent et al., 2021)</ref> and accentedness rankings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Henry et al., 2024)</ref> in children and adults.

text.text: This parallels developmental findings of gradient recognition of deliberate mispronunciations within the listener's accent, such as producing fish as "fesh" (Creel, 2012; Swingley, 2016; White & Morgan, 2008).
text.formatted: This parallels developmental findings of gradient recognition of deliberate mispronunciations within the listener's accent, such as producing fish as "fesh" <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Creel, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Swingley, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">White & Morgan, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: One factor that improves accented speech recognition is increasing its familiarity.

Familiarity can come from immersion (e.g. Bent & Bradlow, 2003; Xie & Fowler, 2013) or experimental exposure or training (Bradlow & Bent, 2008; Sidaras et al., 2009; see Schmale et al., 2012; White & Aslin, 2011, in infants/toddlers), the latter of which often takes the form of transcribing accented speech.
text.formatted: Familiarity can come from immersion (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bent & Bradlow, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Xie & Fowler, 2013)</ref> or experimental exposure or training <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bradlow & Bent, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sidaras et al., 2009</ref>; see <ref type="bibr">Schmale et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">White & Aslin, 2011</ref>, in infants/toddlers), the latter of which often takes the form of transcribing accented speech.

text.text: Training appears most effective when the listener is trained on the same talker they are tested on (Bradlow & Bent, 2008; Xie et al., 2021), a talker who sounds similar to the test talker (Xie & Myers, 2017), or multiple training talkers (Bradlow & Bent, 2008; Xie et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Training appears most effective when the listener is trained on the same talker they are tested on <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bradlow & Bent, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Xie et al., 2021)</ref>, a talker who sounds similar to the test talker <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Xie & Myers, 2017)</ref>, or multiple training talkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bradlow & Bent, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Xie et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: There is still substantial disagreement about many aspects of accent adaptation, especially about the degree to which exposure generalizes and how exposure variability affects generalization.

Exposure to multiple talkers appears less effective than exposure to the actual test talker (Xie et al., 2021), but it is possible that larger numbers of exposure talkers would yield different results.

text.text: On the far end of exposure variability, one study suggests that multiple-accent exposure can generalize to an untrained accent (Baese-Berk et al. 2013).
text.formatted: On the far end of exposure variability, one study suggests that multiple-accent exposure can generalize to an untrained accent <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baese-Berk et al. 2013</ref>).

text.text: While we do not address adaptation directly in our study, we return to it in the Discussion.
Another factor that improves accented speech recognition is contextual support.

One form of contextual support is semantic cues to upcoming words in a sentence (e.g. banana in The monkey ate the banana vs. the less-supportive The woman saw the banana vs. the rather surprising To cross the river, we walked on a banana).

Sentence context supports recognition of the sentence-final word, both in familiar accented speech (e.g. Altmann & Kamide, 1999; Dahan & Tanenhaus, 2004; Kamide et al., 2003) and unfamiliar-accented speech (Holt & Bent, 2017; Creel, 2012; Creel et al. 2016; Kato & Baese-Berk, 2023).
text.formatted: Sentence context supports recognition of the sentence-final word, both in familiar accented speech (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Altmann & Kamide, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dahan & Tanenhaus, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Kamide et al., 2003)</ref> and unfamiliar-accented speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Holt & Bent, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Creel, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Creel et al. 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kato & Baese-Berk, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Constraining visual context (a small set of pictures to select an answer from, vs. open-set recognition) also appears to improve accented speech processing (Creel et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Constraining visual context (a small set of pictures to select an answer from, vs. open-set recognition) also appears to improve accented speech processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Creel et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Listeners who are better at using context, or have more awareness of context, show larger context benefits; for example, older children (age 7 years) use context more than younger children (5 years; Holt & Bent, 2017).
text.formatted: Listeners who are better at using context, or have more awareness of context, show larger context benefits; for example, older children (age 7 years) use context more than younger children (5 years; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Holt & Bent, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: What these various flavors of contextual support seem to have in common is that they lead human listeners to upweight some word alternatives or downweight others, reducing the difficulty of recognizing an ambiguous or misleading form.
Still, the relative effect sizes of accent strength, perceptual adaptation effects, and contextual support on accented speech recognition remain unclear.
Modern ASR models have been applied to speech of a variety of accents in English, with varying degrees of success (see Kim et al., 2024, for a 4-way comparison).
text.formatted: Modern ASR models have been applied to speech of a variety of accents in English, with varying degrees of success (see <ref type="bibr">Kim et al., 2024, for a 4-way comparison)</ref>.

text.text: Some of the most recent models use massive amounts of data to train both a language (word-prediction) model and a speech model.
Ample text training data in principle provide substantial context knowledge-both local context (rubber predicts ducky, the predicts nouns) and also sentence level and discourselevel context.
Extensive speech training data might also provide exposure to more diverse speech forms including some accented speakers.
Thus, such models have substantial linguistic context built in, and presumably at least some accent exposure that might contribute to "pre-adaptation."
Unlike humans, these large neural network models are "frozen" for general use.

Thus, they can use context within the presented material, but cannot learn contextual patterns or accent regularities over repeated exposure in a study (though see recent work by Roll et al., 2025, on a model that can do in-context adaptation).
text.formatted: Thus, they can use context within the presented material, but cannot learn contextual patterns or accent regularities over repeated exposure in a study (though see recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Roll et al., 2025, on a</ref> model that can do in-context adaptation).

text.text: One prominent example is Whisper, created by OpenAI (Radford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: One prominent example is Whisper, created by OpenAI <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Whisper was designed to generalize across a wide range of language inputs without the need for additional fine-tuning.
Its "weakly supervised" training dataset includes 680,000 hours of audio, 440,000 hours of which consists of English text-speech pairs (Radford et al., 2023) across model sizes.
text.formatted: Its "weakly supervised" training dataset includes 680,000 hours of audio, 440,000 hours of which consists of English text-speech pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref> across model sizes.

text.text: The large model tested here, large-v3, was trained on 5 million hours of audio, mostly (80%) derived from outputs of the large-v2 model. Radford et al. (2023) do not describe the breakdown of accent variation in Whisper's undisclosed English-language training data, but it is believed to contain substantial US-based content, suggesting North American speakers predominate. Radford et al. (2023), the model's creators, report that Whisper has humanlike or even superhuman accuracy on first-language English speech.

text.text: What of accented speech?

Radford et al. (2023) report few direct tests of accents in English, but the accented English subset of VoxPopuli (Wang et al., 2021), a corpus of European parliament recordings, showed heightened transcription error rates relative to error rates on comparable first-language English speech.

(2023)</ref> report few direct tests of accents in English, but the accented English subset of VoxPopuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Wang et al., 2021)</ref>, a corpus of European parliament recordings, showed heightened transcription error rates relative to error rates on comparable first-language English speech.

text.text: Other assessments have been conducted by researchers outside OpenAI, most of which generally suggest good to humanlike Whisper performance based on direct comparison to human transcribers. Kim et al. (2024) report that Whisper outperformed three other models and comparably to humans in transcribing Mandarin-accented English, and McGuire and Larson-Hall (2025) found Whisper performance very similar to human transcribers for Japaneseaccented English.
text.formatted: Other assessments have been conducted by researchers outside OpenAI, most of which generally suggest good to humanlike Whisper performance based on direct comparison to human transcribers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kim et al. (2024)</ref> report that Whisper outperformed three other models and comparably to humans in transcribing Mandarin-accented English, and McGuire and Larson-Hall (2025) found Whisper performance very similar to human transcribers for Japaneseaccented English.

text.text: Additionally, in both studies, humans and Whisper tended to transcribe the same speakers more accurately vs. less accurately, suggesting similar sensitivity to variation in accent strength or speech clarity. Graham and Roll (2024) found that transcription accuracy for second-language English speakers increases with speakers' English experience, and that Whisper is slightly more accurate on North American English than British or Australian accents, consistent with Whisper being specialized to North American English.

text.text: While most of the foregoing work on accent variation in English suggests only modest difficulty for Whisper, work on other less-represented speech forms implies substantial underperformance by Whisper and other ASR systems, a literature worth examining for parallels to accented speech processing.

One such case where performance is notably poor is child speech. McGonigle et al. (2024) reported relatively high error rates in speech from typically-developing 2-3-year-olds (50%) and even higher error rates in 2-5-year-olds with Down syndrome (86%). Bradley et al. (2025) found that voice assistants (Siri, Alexa) systematically underperform humans on young child speech (2-5-year-olds).
text.formatted: One such case where performance is notably poor is child speech. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">McGonigle et al. (2024)</ref> reported relatively high error rates in speech from typically-developing 2-3-year-olds (50%) and even higher error rates in 2-5-year-olds with Down syndrome (86%). <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bradley et al. (2025)</ref> found that voice assistants (Siri, Alexa) systematically underperform humans on young child speech (2-5-year-olds).

text.text: Relatedly, Fan et al. (2024) and Attia et al. (2024) report that Whisper requires fine-tuning to reduce (US English) child-speech transcription error rates. Zhang et al. (2026) test 12 ASR systems and find worse performance on both child and older adult speech, and extremely poor performance on dysarthric speech.

(2024)</ref> report that Whisper requires fine-tuning to reduce (US English) child-speech transcription error rates. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Zhang et al. (2026)</ref> test 12 ASR systems and find worse performance on both child and older adult speech, and extremely poor performance on dysarthric speech.

text.text: Thus, while Whisper appears reasonably successful on highly represented non-US accents in English in the sense that it is comparable to human listeners, it is still the most accurate when transcribing US English.

Other speech varieties that are underrepresented in ASR models' training data (child speech, speech from individuals with dysarthria or nonfluent aphasia) may suffer even more substantial ASR deficits, potentially limiting the systems' usefulness for those speakers.
This accent deficit highlights the need for better understanding of model generalization, and linguistic factors that may mitigate its accent difficulties.
The above evidence suggests that Whisper performs, if not well, to a humanlike degree on at least some accented speech forms.
However, it is not clear what model features allow Whisper to do so: leveraging word predictions from its language model; high quality, adaptable phonetic processing; or both.
Probing the role of the system's language model requires assessing its performance in more vs. less predictable contexts.
If Whisper succeeds in part by leveraging its language model, it should perform better when sentence context is available.

"Context" might include both sentence level semantic context (The monkey ate the…) and local context that identifies, say, form class (noun, verb, etc.): for example, English "the" commonly precedes nouns and rarely precedes verbs.

If Whisper excels at phonetic processing, especially if it has substantial exposure in its underdescribed training data to Spanish accents that are prevalent in the US, then it should be successful regardless of context, that is, even on single words-or its error patterns, like humans', should at least strongly resemble phonetic form.
For example, errors for Spanish-accented "bag" might include "back" (a single-phonetic-feature change) but not "bye" (a multi-feature, multi-phoneme change).

While many studies of large language models (LLMs) have investigated word predictability extensively, we are not aware of other studies that probe the recent wave of LLM-powered speech recognition systems with varying degrees of predictability.
In the current work, we capitalized on SAUCE, a set of speech materials that were developed and recorded one decade ago in our lab.

Development of these sentences is detailed below, but briefly, its 300 sentences were spoken by 20 speakers, half of whom spoke English with a second language (L2) accent from Spanish, and the other half a first language (L1) US accent.

To our knowledge, SAUCE is unique amongst speech datasets used to evaluate Whisper in that it specifically assays Spanish accents, the most common variety of second language accent in the US (US Census Bureau, 2023).
SAUCE also appears unique amongst datasets testing Whisper in containing variation in target-word sensicality, allowing us to test model performance as a function of sensicality.

A third feature of SAUCE is that, unlike the Hearing In Noise Test (HINT; Nilsson et al., 1994) used in Kim et al. (2024) or similar sentence sets in widespread use in speech sciences research, there is virtually no possibility that these sentences are included in Whisper's voluminous but uncharacterized training data because this sentence set, which prior to this year was published only on our lab web site in text format, has received little scientific attention to date, and none of our recordings are published online.

(2024)</ref> or similar sentence sets in widespread use in speech sciences research, there is virtually no possibility that these sentences are included in Whisper's voluminous but uncharacterized training data because this sentence set, which prior to this year was published only on our lab web site in text format, has received little scientific attention to date, and none of our recordings are published online.

text.text: Because of the relative obscurity of this sentence set, then, Whisper cannot inflate performance via prior exposure to the SAUCE sentences.
We focused on accuracy of the target (final) word.
We assessed accent sensitivity by comparing final word accuracy on Spanish-accented vs.
US-accented materials.

We gauged sensitivity to sentence context by looking at accuracy for final words transcribed in sentence context vs. final words that had been excised from sentence contexts, with sentence contexts of varying (non)sensicality.
These investigations stand to advance understanding of both machine and human processing of accents.
Possible benefits to models include highlighting cases where humans may still exceed or differ from model performance.

In the opposite direction, our investigation speaks to the extent to which ASR models are a reasonable stand-in for human accent processing; if they are, then ASR models might be used to tirelessly explore the full space of accent exposure regimes via training or fine-tuning.
We return to this point in the Discussion.
This collection included 300 unique sentences: 100 sensical, 100 nonsensical, and 100 containing nonwords, structured to end in one of 100 target words.
Initially, sensical sentences (e.g.
"The monkey ate the banana", target word underlined) were generated based on a set of target words.
Sentence stems were then normed for word completion on adults (N = 23 L1 English speakers), and then children (N = 26-29 L1 English learners per sentence, who responded verbally).
The 100 most predictable items were selected.
For the final set of sentences, adult cloze probabilities had a mean of 88% (SD = 15%; range 35%-100%), while child cloze probabilities averaged 57%, (SD = 23%; range 19%-96%).
Nonsensical sentences were created by scrambling target words across sentence stems, yielding sentences like The monkey ate the shark.

Lastly, to generate even more difficult to parse sentences, the 100 nonsensical sentences were altered by swapping word onsets with a different content word in another sentence stem to place a single pronounceable nonword in the sentence stem, such as The runkey ate the shark.
SAUCE sentences were recorded by 20 speakers, balanced for accent (half U.S.-accented, half Mexican-Spanish accented) and sex (half female, half male).
Spanish-accented speakers were all born in Mexico and reported an age of English onset at 10 years or later (M=14.1±5.8).
They ranged in age from 18-55 years (M=29.6±12.9).
US-accented speakers had learned English from birth, were raised in California, and ranged in age from 18-36 (M=22.6±5.5; one age missing).
Speakers were instructed to avoid using contrastive prosody (e.g.
"The runkey ate the shark.
The monkey ate the banana. …") and to speak slowly and clearly, as if to a child.
Sentences deemed to have nonideal recordings were noted by the researcher and re-recorded.
Recordings were edited by hand so that each sentence was contained in a single file.
Final word boundaries also were marked by hand in Praat text grids by trained researchers, guarding against unnatural truncation that might result from using unedited forced alignments.
Words in isolation were extracted directly from those recorded sentences.
Human transcriptions of the recordings were completed in 2014 to calibrate accent difficulty in planned studies testing child processing of Spanish-vs.
US-accented speech (Creel et al., 2016; see also Creel, 2016).
text.formatted: US-accented speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Creel et al., 2016</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Creel, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In the current study, we repurposed these adult transcriptions to serve as a baseline for machine transcription performance.
Procedure.
Human transcriptions.

To obtain human transcriptions, audio recordings were first presented to a group of native or near-native English speakers (N = 75) unfamiliar with the content, who transcribed each word or sentence recording after a single hearing.
Listeners were compensated with course credit.
Transcriber language background.
All listeners reported learning English at age 5 or earlier (M=1.4, SD=1.9), and the majority (n=45) from age 0.
All reported that English was their dominant language.
Some (n=51) reported learning another language in addition to English at age 5 or earlier, including 7 who also spoke Spanish.
Multilingual listeners performed similarly to monolingual listeners (see human transcription analyses below).
Transcriber accent familiarity.
A post-test questionnaire asked listeners what accents they typically hear around San Diego, as well as what accent(s) they thought they had heard in the study.
The majority (67%) reported hearing Spanishlike accents (broadly construed; e.g.
Mexican, Spanish, Hispanic, Latino, Latin American) in San Diego, plus several other accents represented in San Diego.
Most (80%) also reported hearing Spanishlike accents in the study itself-but a sizeable number (36%) reported hearing some other accent instead of or in addition to a Spanishlike accent.
Only 55% reported a Spanishlike accent and no other accent (not counting L1 US accents).
This spurious accent reporting suggests that our listeners' exposure to Spanish accents may be limited overall, given that it is not sufficient to confer strong recognizability of Spanish accents.
Twenty-five listeners were assigned to each sentence type.
Each listener heard 500 audio files total, half sentences, half single words.

In each block of 100 randomly ordered trials (50 sentences and 50 single words intermixed), a given listener only heard a particular sentence or word a single time, so for the first 100 trials, they were hearing each item for the first time, and they heard a given sentence or final word 5 times total.
The ratio of Spanish-accented to USaccented items was 80:20.

The original logic behind this ratio, given that the adult transcriptions were part of a stimulus intelligibility norming study for child experiments, was to fully explore the less familiar accent stimuli to gauge a wide range of intelligibility.

This decision does mean that human listeners had more opportunity to adapt to the Spanish-accented speech, which may have relatively improved transcription in Spanish accented speech, decreasing accent effects.
Thus our findings may be an overestimate of "naïve" Spanish accent transcription accuracythough, as apparent below, Spanish accent transcription was less accurate than US accent transcription.
ASR model and procedure.
The neural network family employed in this study is Whisper, in five different model sizes (tiny, base, small, medium, and large-v3; Radford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The neural network family employed in this study is Whisper, in five different model sizes (tiny, base, small, medium, and large-v3; <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Radford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We selected Whisper for this study because of its demonstrated capabilities in processing second language accents in noise (Kim et al., 2024), as well as overall impressive performance (Radford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: We selected Whisper for this study because of its demonstrated capabilities in processing second language accents in noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kim et al., 2024)</ref>, as well as overall impressive performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the model is available for local (not web-based) use, a necessity as we did not have explicit consent to submit our speakers' recordings to an external ASR transcription service.
We tested all five model sizes to assess whether increased model complexity facilitates accented speech processing or context use.

All audio files were processed through five sizes of the Whisper speech recognition system (tiny, base, small, medium, and large-v3) to evaluate machine transcription capabilities and the extent to which they change with model size.

In the fall of 2023, we downloaded the Whisper model from GitHub (https://github.com/openai/whisper) and then used a Python script to read in a directory of audio files, iterate them through each model size, and output predicted text.
text.formatted: In the fall of 2023, we downloaded the Whisper model from GitHub (<ref type="url" target="https://github.com/openai/whisper">https://github.com/openai/whisper</ref>) and then used a Python script to read in a directory of audio files, iterate them through each model size, and output predicted text.

text.text: The language was set to English (en).
Given that Whisper's outputs are deterministic, each individual audio file was transcribed once per model size.

This coincided with a single transcription per human, since audio files were distributed across human transcribers (each occurred five times across five blocks of transcription trials, but as noted below, we only considered the first block of human transcriptions to avoid repeated-stimulus benefits).
We used only the first 100 transcriptions per human, which did not contain stimulus repeats, in order to more closely match the Whisper model's lack of capacity to learn from repetition.

For example, a human might hear "The monkey ate the shark" clearly within the first 100 transcription trials, and then transcribe the same sentence accurately when it occurs in the second group of 100 trials because they are biased toward memory of the first instance rather than accurately perceiving the second instance.
This memory bias differs from general phonetic adaptation.
The machine listener cannot memorize previously heard sentences or words, nor can it adapt.

Of course, the machine model does not experience fatigue effects either, so the decision to use earlier human transcription trials also limits the possibility that human transcription accuracy is lowered by fatigue (visible in our own data; see Figure S7).
text.formatted: Of course, the machine model does not experience fatigue effects either, so the decision to use earlier human transcription trials also limits the possibility that human transcription accuracy is lowered by fatigue (visible in our own data; see Figure <ref type="figure">S7</ref>).

text.text: Analyses focused on the final word in each sentence, or the isolated final words.
Note that accuracy for single words is a binary value (0 or 1).
See Supplemental Materials for sentence-stem accuracy results.
Exclusions and data cleaning.
Word accuracy as a measure is inflexible to certain types of transcriptions that we deemed phonetically acceptable.
Approximately 2.3% of analyzed transcriptions were updated after automated final-word accuracy calculations.
As we did not know what alternate spellings to expect a priori, we maintained running logs of homophones and common misspellings.
Given the open-ended nature of transcription, experimenter judgment was occasionally necessary.
For human participants and models, we systematically rescored homophone "errors" (for instance, aunt instead of ant; b or be instead of bee) as correct.

We also hand-rescored human spelling errors as correct (e.g. rubber duckie for rubber ducky; several spellings of dinosaur, motorcycle, and banana) as well as human errors that were clearly typos (tbale, which is unpronounceable in both English and Spanish, for table) and the target word "rubber ducky", which foiled our accuracy calculations because it contained a space.

However, we retained as errors cases where the transcription implied a different pronunciation or word (e.g. snowmen for snowman; relatedly, note that morphological variants with different pronunciations were counted as errors, such as snowman/*snowmen or shoes/*shoe).

Most of the updates were accounted for by scoring errors or alternate spellings on the noun compound "rubber ducky" (30.1% of updates), and the six words bee, witch, nose, cereal, ants, and carrot (another 63.0% of updates), each of which had one or more homophonous spellings.
The remainder (6.9% of updates, or 0.16% of total transcriptions) included a mixture of homophones, misspellings, and typos.

For Whisper, a small proportion of trials (n=9) included looping errors, where the same brief phrase repeated multiple times (e.g. for one recording of the word "zebra", the phrase "See you soon in the next video." occurred 22 times in a row).
These errors are acknowledged in the original paper (Radford et al., 2023) and noted by Kim et al. (2024).
text.formatted: These errors are acknowledged in the original paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Radford et al., 2023)</ref> and noted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kim et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: We marked any machine transcriptions with a character length greater than 100 as "looping" and excluded these.
Humans did not produce looping errors.
Analyses.
There were three sets of statistical models.
For each, the dependent variable is the accuracy (0 or 1) of the sentence-final target word.
We first present findings from human transcribers.
This allows confirmation that human results largely replicate prior work, setting the context for ASR model outcomes.
Next, we examine performance of the Whisper model itself, including assessment of effects of model size (five levels from tiny to large-v3).
Last, we compare the humans and Whisper (large-v3) to examine potential human-machine divergences.
All statistical models assessed effects of accent (US English, Mexican Spanish), sentence sensicality (sensical, nonsensical, nonword), and sentence context (word in sentence context, isolated word).
We had a small set of basic questions about model transcription behavior.
First, does the ASR system experience difficulty in processing less-familiar accents in English, and is accent difficulty modulated by varying levels of support from sentence context?
Second, how similar are human performance and model performance?

We computed a series of logistic mixed-effects models on accuracy with predictors Accent (mean-centered; US = .5, Spanish = -.5), Sentence Sensicality (Helmert-coded: one contrast compared sensical sentences with the combination of the other two, and the other compared nonsensical sentences with nonword-containing sentences), and Context (word in sentence = .5, isolated word = -.5).
Additional predictors are included as described.
To circumvent convergence issues, we included maximal main effects random slopes for listeners, talkers, and words, but removed random effects correlations.
We report beta (B) values as a measure of effect size.
To contextualize the ASR system findings, we first describe human transcription results (Figures 1 and 2), which largely concur with existing findings reviewed above.
text.formatted: To contextualize the ASR system findings, we first describe human transcription results (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref>), which largely concur with existing findings reviewed above.

text.text: We computed a logistic mixed-effects regression model on accuracy with Accent, Sentence Sensicality, and Context as predictors.

While our human listeners were first-language or early learners of English, many had multilingual experience, so we also included Language Background (monolingual = .5, multilingual = -.5) and its interactions.
Accent was significant (B = 0.95, SE = 0.24, z = 3.92, p < .0001), with higher accuracy for US accented words.
text.formatted: Accent was significant (B = 0.95, SE = 0.24, z = 3.92, p < .0001), with higher accuracy for US accented words.

text.text: Context was also significant (B = 0.69, SE = 0.17, z = 4.13, p < .0001), with higher accuracy for words in sentences vs. isolated words.
text.formatted: Context was also significant (B = 0.69, SE = 0.17, z = 4.13, p < .0001), with higher accuracy for words in sentences vs. isolated words.

text.text: The high Sentence Sensicality contrast was significant (B = 0.83, SE = 0.21, z = 3.98, p < .0001), with overall higher accuracy for words drawn from sensical sentences.

text.text: Standard errors are calculated over means for individual words (n=100 per data point).

Language Background was not significant (B = 0.03, SE = 0.17, z = 0.17, p = .87), meaning that multilingual speakers neither benefited nor suffered detectably overall from their more diverse language experiences.

Additionally, none of the 11 interaction terms involving Language Background were significant, including Language Background x Accent (B = 0.20, SE = 0.30, z = 0.69, p = .49), suggesting that being multilingual did not confer selective advantages for accented speech.

One interaction was marginal, Context x Sentence Type x Language Background (B = 1.42, SE = 0.73, z = 1.93, p = .053), suggesting that the relative sensicalsentence context benefit was slightly milder for multilingual listeners (see Supplementary Figure S6).

In short, L2 accents decreased human accuracy, sensical sentence stems but not other stems increased accuracy over isolated words, and listener language experience outside English did not convincingly affect accuracy.

Sensicality interacted (B = -0.30, SE = 0.14, z = -2.13, p = .03), not observed in human transcribers, such that words from sensical sentences were more accurate overall but the benefit was larger for Spanish accents than US English accents.

This was qualified by a 3-way interaction of Accent, Sentence Sensicality, and Context (B = -1.04, SE = 0.28, z = -3.72, p = .0002), also absent in human data, such that the sentence-context boost for sensical over nonsensical/nonword sentences was relatively greater for Spanish accents.

This three-way interaction was further qualified by a four-way interaction with Whisper Size (B = -0.46, SE = 0.19, z = -2.43, p = .02), such that the greater sentence benefit for sensical sentences did not change in magnitude for US accents as model size increased (B = -0.22, SE = 0.20, z = -1.12, p = .26), but increased in magnitude for Spanish accents as model size increased (B = 0.25, SE = 0.07, z = 3.57, p = .0004). in sentences (solid) and in isolation) dotted.

text.text: Further explorations.
The large data set afforded a number of interesting explorations, detailed in the Supplementary Materials.
The most important of these addresses the conditions underlying Whisper's nonsense-sentence benefit.
First, we tested the "short context facilitation" hypothesis of the nonsensical words-in-sentences benefit for Whisper.
We did this by increasing the amount of preceding nonsensical sentence context, from 0 preceding words to 1 to 2 to ~2.5.

Longer contexts led to incremental gains in final-word recognition, but did not reach ceiling (full sentence context) accuracy, suggesting that low-level word prediction (e.g. "the …" predicts a noun) cannot fully explain the words-in-sentences benefit.

Relatedly, Zhang et al. (2026) have recently reported increases in accuracy with sentence length in Dutch sentences in 12 different ASR systems including Whisper, suggesting that the words-in-sentences benefit may represent a more general property of LLM-based predictions rather than being unique to Whisper.
text.formatted: Relatedly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Zhang et al. (2026)</ref> have recently reported increases in accuracy with sentence length in Dutch sentences in 12 different ASR systems including Whisper, suggesting that the words-in-sentences benefit may represent a more general property of LLM-based predictions rather than being unique to Whisper.

text.text: Second, we delved into Whisper's unusual error patterns on single words, and found that it appears to contain "attractor basins" toward certain highly probable short conversational utterances, for example, "Thank you," "Thanks for watching," "Here," "Bye," and "See you bro."

In short, we suspect that the reason for Whisper's nonsense sentence stem benefit is that its word prediction system actively distorts speech processing for very short utterances (in this case, single words).
In the current study we asked two questions.
First, how does Whisper perform on Spanishaccented English compared to US-accented English, and how does this interact with sentence context?
As with other previously investigated accents, Whisper shows a deficit in transcribing Spanish-accented English relative to US English.

Whisper also performs better on words in sensical sentence contexts, with particularly strong benefits for Spanish-accented speech, suggesting that sentence context helps it generalize outside its (presumed) training data.
We are not aware of previous work on recent ASR systems that considers sentence predictability, or the conjunction of predictability and accent variation.
We also asked about the extent of similarities to human processing, an important question if we wish to use ASR systems as "model organisms" to study human accent processing and adaptation.

Whisper performed similarly to human listeners in multiple respects: both human and machine transcribers performed better on US accents and in sensical sentence contexts, and talkers who were better transcribed by humans were also better transcribed by Whisper.

This last point echoes findings in Mandarin-accented (Kim et al., 2024) and Japanese-accented (McGuire & Larson-Hall, 2025) English speakers, and suggests that Whisper transcription error rates might be a reasonable working analogy to human listeners' degree of difficulty in understanding speakers, an implication we explore below.
text.formatted: This last point echoes findings in Mandarin-accented <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kim et al., 2024)</ref> and Japanese-accented (McGuire & Larson-Hall, 2025) English speakers, and suggests that Whisper transcription error rates might be a reasonable working analogy to human listeners' degree of difficulty in understanding speakers, an implication we explore below.

text.text: Unlike humans, though, Whisper shows a boost in final-word transcription performance from all sentence contexts, not just sensical ones, a finding that we have not seen reported previously.

We suggest that Whisper's good performance in sentence contexts and variable performance in single-word contexts are both ascribable to its language model, which helps in longer sentence contexts, but in shorter contexts leads Whisper astray due to apparent attractor basins for very short utterances.

This makes some sense if we believe that Whisper is trained on conversational speech, which does not contain a great deal of bare content words ("zebra") but does contain interjections ("see ya bro").
From this perspective, Whisper's short-utterance attractors are conforming to its training data.
In itself, conforming to training data is unsurprising
Whisper performs as well as English-dominant listeners on sentential Spanish-accented English.
However, it appears to have more difficulty with isolated words than one might expect from its in-sentence performance, and it makes isolated word errors that differ qualitatively from humans.'

One possibility is that its language (word-prediction) model may hold back speech processing capability by misleadingly restricting the probability space for short utterances (see Further explorations, above, and Supplement).
Model fine-tuning, or more length-diverse and accent-diverse training data from the outset, might reduce single-word errors.
A few findings suggest ways of accelerating research on human accent adaptation, focused on the high similarity between humans' and Whisper's transcription accuracy at the talker level.

First, Whisper (as well as other ASR models) might aid researchers by providing a ranking of talkers by intelligibility-at least, within speakers of the same accent-without the need to conduct the time-consuming norming transcription procedures which are often a precursor to studies of accent adaptation.

In addition to saving time, Whisper gets around lingering concerns that human transcription or human reports of understanding accented speakers may implicitly include social judgment (e.g. Kang & Rubin, 2009), as ASR models do not embody complex social knowledge.
text.formatted: In addition to saving time, Whisper gets around lingering concerns that human transcription or human reports of understanding accented speakers may implicitly include social judgment (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kang & Rubin, 2009)</ref>, as ASR models do not embody complex social knowledge.

text.text: As a theoretical aside, ASRs' lack of social knowledge sheds light on human accent perception itself: to the extent that ASR makes errors resembling human listeners', perhaps human accent misunderstanding occurs mostly for reasons of perceptual inexperience, rather than social bias.

We do not mean to discount the bias inherent in creating models that underrepresent some speech forms, but to suggest that ASR transcription findings further support a predominantly perceptual basis for human accented speech processing difficulties.

Second, the resemblance at the talker level between Whisper and human transcription also suggests the possibility of testing out a wide range of accent adaptation hypotheses by finetuning ASR systems with different types of speech input.

Even limiting consideration to accents in English-which we think is too limiting!-the possible combinations of numbers of speakers, accent varieties, training content, training durations, and types of generalization could require millions of hours of human participant time.
ASR systems could be used to explore this space both rapidly and methodically, followed by targeted reliability checks with humans.
However, we cannot recommend Whisper across all English-language situations because some of its behaviors diverge from those of human transcribers.
In particular, its susceptibility to lexical or short-phrase biases (see Supplement for details) makes it less than ideal for detailed speech tasks involving single words or short utterances.

text.text: Several limitations are worth pointing out here.
First, we tested only one second-language English accent, Spanish.
The use of only two accents limits our ability to generalize to other accents (e.g.
Dutch-accented or Yoruba-accented English) or languages (e.g. both Yoruba and Dutch accents in both Yoruba and Dutch languages).
Second, our sentence speech materials are not reflective of natural conversational speech.
In particular, the nonsensical and nonwordcontaining sentences, while useful for probing contextual facilitation of word recognition, are anomalous with respect to everyday language.
Future work should examine sentences with a wider range of predictability and plausibility, as well as lengthier discourses.
Third, the binary word accuracy measure-while frequently used in many accented speech studies and in assessment of ASR model performance-does not capture the details of partial phonetic matches.
For example, for the word bed, both "bet" and "that" are errors at the word level, but "bet" is closer phonetically.
A phonetic edit distance measure might better define performance, and possibly give an edge to humans, by awarding partial credit to similar-sounding-word errors.
Fourth, our transcription task presented Spanish:US accented stimuli in a 4:1 ratio (see rationale in Method), possibly narrowing accent familiarity effects.

Fifth, we obtained only granular information about human listeners' Spanish-accented speech experience; while many of them recognized accented stimuli as Spanish (and, often, some other accent that was not actually present), the actual amount of exposure was not quantified.
These limitations could be addressed in future work.
As noted above, we see future directions both for ASR modeling of diverse speech forms, and for simulation work to understand human accent adaptation.

For ASR models, either better representation across accents needs to be included in training data, or, less elegantly, a range of models need to be fine-tuned to particular accents-and to short utterances.

For human accent adaptation research, ASR models might serve as a tool to assess relative talker intelligibility, and perhaps a platform to explore the full space of accent adaptation regimes in humans, with targeted human follow-up studies.
